subject: history
title: Persecution and Resistance Adventure
welcome_lead: Today you'll witness Nazi persecution of Jews and the few who dared resist.
meta_desc: GCSE History — Nuremberg Laws, Kristallnacht, Holocaust and resistance.
final_note: You learned how persecution escalated to genocide and who tried to resist.

walkthroughs.body_html:
A boycott of Jewish shops on 1 April 1933 began legal persecution.

The Nuremberg Laws of 1935 stripped Jews of citizenship and banned marriage with 'Aryans'. By 1938 Jews could not own businesses or attend German schools.

On 9-10 November 1938 Nazis smashed 7,500 Jewish shops and burned synagogues on Kristallnacht.

30,000 Jewish men were sent to camps. After the 1942 Wannsee Conference the Final Solution began at Auschwitz, Treblinka and other death camps. About 6 million Jews were murdered.

Resistance was rare and risky. The Edelweiss Pirates brawled with Hitler Youth.

Hans and Sophie Scholl's White Rose handed out leaflets in Munich — they were beheaded in February 1943. On 20 July 1944 Colonel Stauffenberg's bomb at the Wolf's Lair failed to kill Hitler. 5,000 conspirators were executed.

mcqs.q: How did Hitler come to power in 1933?
options: He was legally appointed Chancellor by President Hindenburg as part of a conservative political deal, after the Nazis became the largest party in the Reichstag.
Hitler seized power through a violent coup or revolution.
Hitler won an outright majority in the 1932 presidential election.
The Nuremberg Laws were the post-war trial of Nazi leaders.

mcqs.q: What was the political significance of the Reichstag Fire?
options: Hitler personally set the fire and blamed it on the Communists.
The fire destroyed all of Berlin and forced people to support the Nazis.
Hitler won an outright majority in the 1932 presidential election.
Hitler used it to issue the Reichstag Fire Decree suspending civil liberties, jail Communists, and create the conditions for the Enabling Act of March 1933.

mcqs.q: What did the 1935 Nuremberg Laws do?
options: The Nuremberg Laws sent Jews directly to concentration camps.
The Nuremberg Laws were the post-war trial of Nazi leaders.
They stripped German Jews of citizenship and banned marriage or sexual relations between Jews and 'Aryans', defining Jewishness racially rather than religiously.
Hitler won an outright majority in the 1932 presidential election.
